turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: All right. So next we need to go to the ideas layer and the ideas layer is there to help us sort through the many ideas we might encounter and they may come from as you said the founders, the managers, the stakeholders, from the team, from research, from competitors. We're flooded with ideas, and what usually happens inside organization is some sort of battle of opinions or some sort of politics sometimes or highest paid person's opinion. You had, Ronny Kohavi, who invented this term in your show. What doesn't happen is very rational, logical decisions these are the best ideas, because it's really, really hard to predict honestly. There is so much uncertainty in the needs of the users, in the changes in the market, in our technology, in our product, in our own organization. It's almost impossible to say this idea is going to be the best, but we do say this because we have cognitive biases that kind of convince us that this idea is far superior to anything else and it's definitely the right choice. (00:34:48): In order to avoid this, what we want to do is to evaluate the ideas in a much more objective and consistent and transparent way. In the book I suggest using ICE, impact, confidence and ease. I think I have a slide coming on this. So impact, confidence and ease which is basically a way to assign three values to each idea. The impact tries to assess how much impact it'll have on the goals and that's why it's so important that we have very clear goals and not many. How we are measuring the ideas on the North Star metric, on the top business KPI, on a local metric of the team. Whatever it is, let's be clear about it and then let's evaluate the ideas against this thing. Ease, is basically the opposite of effort. How easy or hard it's going to be, but both of those are guesstimates, both of those are things we need to estimate. I would argue that just by breaking the question to these two questions we usually have a slightly better discussion than just my idea is better than yours. (00:35:52): But then there's the third element which is confidence, which tries to assess how sure are we or should we be about our first guesstimates about the impact and the ease.
turns.zh: 好的。接下来我们需要进入创意层面。创意层的存在是为了帮助我们筛选出可能遇到的各种创意想法。这些想法可能来自创始人、管理者、利益相关者、团队内部、研究成果或者竞争对手等。我们常常被创意信息淹没，而组织内部通常会出现各种意见争执、政治斗争，或者以最高薪员工的意见为准。正如罗尼·科哈维（Ronny Kohavi）在你的节目中提出的术语，组织内部往往缺乏理性和逻辑的决策。这些都是最棒的创意，因为要准确预测创意效果实在太难了。用户需求、市场变化、技术迭代、产品特性以及组织自身都存在诸多不确定性，想要断定某个创意是最好的，几乎是不可能的。但我们总会这样做，因为认知偏差会让我们坚信某个创意远超其他选择，认为它必然是正确的选择。（00:34:48）为了避免这种情况，我们需要以更加客观、一致和透明的方式评估创意。书中建议使用ICE模型，即影响力、信心和易用性。相信我很快会展示相关幻灯片。影响力、信心和易用性本质上是为每个创意赋予三个维度评分的方式。影响力评估创意对目标的影响程度，因此清晰明确的目标至关重要，且目标不宜过多。无论是北极星指标、顶级业务KPI，还是团队内部的局部指标，都要确保目标明确，然后以此为基准评估创意。易用性与努力程度相反，评估创意的难易程度，但这两者都只是猜测，需要我们进行合理估算。通过将问题拆分为这两个维度，我们的讨论通常会比“我的创意比你的好”更有成效。（00:35:52）但还有第三个要素——信心，旨在评估我们对影响力和易用性初始判断的置信度。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting you use the word ease, because I think it's usually effort. You kind of make it positive, is that an intentional tweak you made?
turns.zh: 你用“易用性”这个词很有趣，我觉得通常应该是“努力程度”。你把它变得积极了，这是故意的调整吗？

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: I'm using the definitions of, Sean Ellis. Sean, invented ICE. You know Sean, I don't know if you've had him yet? But he's-
turns.zh: 我用的是肖恩·埃利斯（Sean Ellis）的定义。肖恩发明了ICE模型。你认识肖恩吗？不知道你是否见过他？但他——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I haven't had him on yet.
turns.zh: 我还没见过他。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: Yeah. For the people who don't know him, Sean, is amazing. He's like one of the fathers of the growth movement, he coined the term growth hacking and he popularized the concept of product market fit.
turns.zh: 是啊。对不了解他的人来说，肖恩非常了不起。他是增长运动之父之一，创造了“增长黑客”这个术语，还推广了产品市场契合度的概念。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: He created ICE, he created a bunch of things that we use in product that we don't even know.
turns.zh: 他发明了ICE模型，还有很多我们在产品中使用却不知道出处的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, I didn't know he came up with ICE. Okay, cool. So the original version of ICE is ease instead of effort.
turns.zh: 哇，我不知道ICE是他发明的。好的，酷。所以最初的ICE模型用的是“易用性”而不是“努力程度”。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: Exactly, yeah.
turns.zh: 没错，就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fun fact.
turns.zh: 有趣的事实。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: A lot of your viewers are wondering where's the R because there's another variant of this culture. RICE, where there's rich as well. I prefer ICE because I prefer to fold the rich into the I for various reasons but both are valid, both are equivalent in a sense.
turns.zh: 很多观众都想知道R在哪里，因为还有另一种文化变体——RICE，里面也有“rich”（富有）这个元素。我个人更偏爱ICE，因为出于种种原因，我更倾向于把“rich”融入到“I”中。但两种说法都行得通，本质上是等价的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm in your boat, that's exactly how I think about it. I think people over complicate this stuff and try to get so many math formulas involved with estimating impact, and I feel like these are just simple heuristics to kind of bubble the best ideas to the top. It doesn't have to be a perfect estimate of impact and confidence and all those things, so I think the simpler is better and it always ends up being a spreadsheet. People always have these tools to estimate these things but it's like a spreadsheet, Google Sheets. Great.
turns.zh: 我完全赞同你的看法。我觉得人们把这事想得太复杂了，老是拿各种数学公式来估算影响力，但这些不过是简单的启发式方法，用来筛选最优方案而已。影响力评估不必精确到极致，保持简单明了就行，最终还是要用电子表格处理。人们开发了各种估算工具，但归根结底还是用Excel表格，比如Google Sheets。挺好的。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: So yeah, you're actually leading me to my next point. So when you come to estimate impact you will realize it's the hardest part. So sometimes it's just a gut feeling and it's a guess and sometimes it's based on some spreadsheet or some analysis and the back of envelope calculation you've done and I think that's legitimate. Sometimes these things do show you some things you didn't think of and sometimes the best case it's based on tests. You actually tested it, you interviewed 12 customers, you show them the thing and out of those only one actually liked it. You should reduce your impact based on that usually, or you do other types of tests. We'll talk about testing in a second. What happens is that people tend to just go with gut instinct and then give themselves a high confidence. They say it's an eight and I'm pretty convinced, so it's eight for confidence and I found this a bit disturbing because it kind of subverts the whole system. (00:38:22): So I wanted to help people realize when they have strong evidence in support of their guesses and when it's weak evidence, how to calculate confidence in a sense. For that I created a tool called the confidence meter, which you can see here this colorful thing and should I go and explain it?
turns.zh: 说到估算影响力，这正是难点所在。有时只能凭直觉猜测，有时则基于数据分析或快速计算。我觉得这两种方法都有价值。有时测试能揭示意想不到的结果，比如你测试了12个客户，展示产品后只有一人喜欢，那就应该降低影响力预期。测试很重要，稍后我们会详细讲讲。问题是人们往往凭直觉给出高置信度，比如说"我很确定这是8分"，但这种做法会破坏整个评估体系。（00:38:22）所以我想帮助大家正确认识：当有强有力的证据支持猜测时，和当证据薄弱时，该如何计算置信度？为此我开发了一个叫"置信度仪"的工具，界面很直观，你可以看到这张彩色图表，我该不该现在就演示一下？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, let's do it. And then again, if you're just listening to this you can check this out on YouTube and you can see the actual slide.
turns.zh: 好的，没问题。如果你只是听讲，可以去YouTube看看实际演示幻灯片。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: All right, awesome. So basically I constructed it a bit like a thermo meter. It goes from very low confidence which is the blue area or the upper right, all the way to high confidence which is the red area and you can see the numbers going from zero to 10. Where zero is very low confidence, we don't know basically anything we're just guessing in the dark and 10 is full confidence. You know for sure this thing is a success, no doubt about it and across the circle I put various classes of evidence you might find along the way. So for example, starting at the top right, all of these blue areas about opinions. It could be your own self-confidence in the idea, your self conviction, you feel it's a great idea. Guess what? Behind every terrible idea that was ever someone thought it was great, that gives you 0.01 out of 10. Maybe you created a shiny pitch deck or a six-page document that explains in detail why this is a great idea. Slightly harder to do but still very low confidence, maybe you connected it to some theme, it's about the blockchain... (00:39:59): Well sorry, the blockchain is out of fashion. What's hot right now?
turns.zh: 好的，我把它设计得有点像温度计。从极低置信度（右上角蓝色区域）到极高置信度（红色区域），数值从0到10。0代表极低置信度，完全靠猜测；10代表完全确定。整个圆周上，我标注了可能遇到的不同证据等级。例如，从右上角开始，蓝色区域代表观点。可能是你对自己的创意信心满满，或者觉得这是个好主意。别忘了，很多失败的创意当初也被视为天才之作。这部分得0分。比如你制作了华丽的Pitch Deck，六页长文详细说明其优点，但这类努力得分更低。再比如你把它和某个热门主题结合，比如区块链……（00:39:59）抱歉，区块链已经过时了。现在流行什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: AI.
turns.zh: 人工智能。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: Exactly, AI. It's about AI, that makes it a good idea? Absolutely not. Or the strategy of the company, that's another thematic support. Thousands and thousands of terrible ideas are being implemented right now as we speak based on these themes. So all these things combined can give you a maximum 0.1 out of 10 according to the tool, if you follow it then we move into slightly harder tests. One is reviewing it with your colleagues, your managers, your stakeholders the idea. They don't know it either, they don't have a crystal ball, they're usually not the users, they cannot predict. But they can evaluate it in a slightly more objective way and maybe find flaws in your idea. On the other hand groups tend to have biases too, politics group thing. So groups can actually arrive sometimes with worse decisions than individuals, there's some research to that. Next, our estimates and plans. So you may do some sort of back of the envelope calculation or your colleagues might go out and try to evaluate the ease a little bit better. (00:41:07): That gives you a little bit more confidence, but still we're at the level of guesswork at this point. Next we're moving to data and data could be anecdotal. So you find a few data points dotted across your data or you talk to a handful of customers or maybe one competitor has that same idea. In many companies I meet, if the leading competitor has this feature and we think it's a good idea validation is done. Let's launch it, that's it. It's a great idea, we need to do it. It never works honestly, you should not assume that your competitor actually knows what they're doing anymore than you do. Data could be also what I call market data. That comes from surveys, from assessing a lot of your data by doing a deep competitive analysis and there are other methods where you create a larger dataset and you contrast your idea against it. Finally, to gain medium and high confidence you really need to build your idea and test it and that's where the red area is. (00:42:11): So there's various forms of tests, we'll talk about them if we have time and they give you various levels of confidence.
turns.zh: 没错，就是人工智能。这就能说明它是个好点子吗？绝对不是。或者说公司的战略，这也是另一个支持点。但目前基于这些主题，成千上万糟糕的点子正在被实施。所以综合起来，根据这个工具，你最多能给它打0.1分（满分10分）。如果你照做，那么我们会进入更困难的测试阶段。首先，你要和同事、经理、利益相关者一起评估这个想法。他们也不知道未来，通常不是用户，无法预测。但他们能更客观地评价你的想法，或许还能发现其缺陷。另一方面，团队也容易有偏见，比如政治因素。因此，团队有时做出的决策比个人更糟糕，这方面有研究支持。接下来是我们的估算和计划。你可能会做些粗略计算，或者同事会去更仔细评估可行性。（00:41:07）：这能让你更有信心，但目前仍处于猜测阶段。接下来是数据，数据可能是零星的。比如你在数据中找到几个数据点，或者与少数客户交流，或许竞争对手也有同样的想法。在我接触的许多公司，如果领先的竞争对手有这个功能，而我们认为这是个好点子，就会直接上线。我们总以为这是个好主意，但说实话，这从不奏效。你不应想当然地认为竞争对手比你更懂行。数据还可能是我所说的市场数据。这些数据来自调查，通过深入的竞争分析评估大量数据，还有其他方法，比如创建更大的数据集，将你的想法与之对比。最后，要获得中等和高水平的信心，你确实需要构建并测试你的想法，这部分用红色区域标注。（00:42:11）：所以测试有多种形式，如果有时间我们会详细讲解，它们能给你不同程度的信心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome, this is a very cool visual. We'll link to a image of this in the show notes too if people want to check it out. I think what's awesome about this is you could just use this as a little tool on your team of just like where are we along the spectrum? We think the impact of this is very high. But we're probably in this blue area of confidence and so let's just make sure we understand that and it's really clear language to help people understand. I see if we had this, it'd be a lot more confident.
turns.zh: 太棒了，这个可视化图表很酷。我们也会在节目笔记中附上图片链接，如果大家想查看的话。我觉得很棒的地方在于，你可以把它当作团队的小工具，了解我们在信心曲线上的位置。我们认为这个想法的影响力很高。但我们可能处于蓝色信心区域，所以我们需要确认这一点，而且语言清晰易懂，帮助人们理解。我觉得如果我们有这个工具，信心会更足。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: So you can also tie your investment into the idea based on the level of confidence you had found essentially, so early on you want to do the cheap stuff just to gain more confidence and then you can go and invest more. If it's a really cheap idea, you can jump to a high confidence idea, you can test, you can do an AB experiment. Early adopter program, whatever it is and then launch it. Some ideas you don't need to test, sometimes the expert opinion is enough. If you're just changing the order of the settings, no one sees this or no one will be impacted. The risk is low, you can launch it without testing. So part of the trick is also knowing when to stop, not just trying to force your way all the way up when you don't have to.
turns.zh: 所以你也可以根据找到的信心水平来投入资源，早期阶段先做些低成本测试来获取更多信心，然后再投入更多资金。如果是个成本很低的想法，你可以跳到高信心阶段，进行测试、做A/B实验、开展早期用户计划等等。有些想法无需测试，有时专家意见就足够了。比如只是调整设置顺序，没有人会注意到或受到影响。风险很低，可以不测试就上线。所以关键还在于知道何时停止，而不是一味强求。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really important point. The other important point here is just a big part of a PM's job is to say no and to stop stupid shit from happening and this is an awesome tool to help you do that. To be like, okay, here's this idea you have, just like let's just be real, how confident are we in this? And, okay, it's going to take us three months to do this. Maybe we should think about something different, maybe we should work up the confidence meter before we actually commit to this.
turns.zh: 这确实是个很重要的观点。另一个关键点在于，产品经理的工作核心就是说"不"，阻止愚蠢的决策。这款工具能有效助你达成目标。比如你可以说："好吧，你提的这个想法，先说实话，我们对它的把握度有多大？"或者"要实现这个目标得花三个月时间，或许我们该考虑其他方案，先提升信心再行动。"

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: Yeah. This is a real world usage that I hear about a lot, some people use this to kind of do... An objective way to say no and gently. Or to say we'll think about it but look at these other ideas we have and how their impacting is and confidence stack up.
turns.zh: 没错。这是我常听到的现实场景，人们用它来委婉拒绝，或是说"我们再考虑考虑"，同时评估其他想法的可行性和信心指数。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Classic PM move, just like that was a great idea but what about this better idea? Coming back to something that we talked a bit about at the beginning, say you have a founder who's actually very smart and experienced. Say even at a startup where you don't really have the time to build tons of evidence for ideas. Do you have a different perspective on how much time to spend building confidence in ideas versus just like cool, they actually have really good ideas let's just see what happens?
turns.zh: 典型的产品经理思维：虽然这个主意不错，但我们能否优化一下？回到开头提到的观点——面对聪明且经验丰富的创始人，尤其是在初创公司资源有限、无法为创意积累大量证据的情况下，如何平衡快速验证与深思熟虑的决策？

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: So there's always like a trade-off between speed of delivery and speed of discovery, and that actually leads to the next layer of how do we combine the two? Because people tend to think it's an either/or. Either we are building very fast or we are learning and then we're building very slow, but I think we're using the wrong metric. The metric is not how fast can we get the bits into production, when there's a lot of uncertainty and we all face uncertainty and startup especially. It's not about getting the bits to production, it's about getting the right bits to production. It's about creating the outcomes that you need, the impact, and so it's about time to outcomes and I would argue that the evidence guided method is far more impactful. It's far faster, it's far more resource efficient than the opinion-based method. Because opinion-based methods tend to waste a lot more of your resources, building the wrong things or discovering, learning too late. Well, evidence guided helps you learn earlier. (00:45:50): Plus it is a fallacy that if you learn you don't build, good teams know how to do both at the same time and that's actually what the steps layer is meant to teach you or to help you do.
turns.zh: 速度与深度的权衡取舍才是关键。人们常认为二者非此即彼：要么快速迭代，要么慢条斯理。但我认为我们选错了衡量标准。关键不在于能多快将代码上线（毕竟初创公司面临诸多不确定性），而在于确保上线的是正确的代码，创造出有价值的成果。换句话说，要关注从想法到成果的转化效率。证据导向的方法远比基于主观判断的方法高效得多，因为后者往往浪费大量资源，开发错误产品或在研发后期才发现问题。证据导向能帮助你更早获得反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So maybe just to close off that loop, say someone listening is at a bigger company, say Netflix versus a series A, series B or startup. Is there something you'd recommend about them approaching this differently? Any kind of guidance there of just how to take what you're sharing differently if you're a different source of companies like that?
turns.zh: 太棒了。最后再总结一下，假设听众在大公司（比如Netflix）而非初创公司，处于A轮或B轮融资阶段，有什么建议吗？对于这类公司，如何灵活应用你分享的经验？

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: Absolutely. I think the concept we talked about of the North Star metric, the value created versus the value captured is very important in every company. Building your entire metrics trees, maybe overkill, doing heavy weighted OKRs may be overkill for early stage. Early stage companies even don't know how they create value, so they need to iterate and their goals is really to find product market fit. Beyond that, what happens is that you need to start building your business model. So that's your goal and you iterate towards that and you need to put metrics on that and then when you move into scale, you need to try to create order because when you scale up... And all of this is covered in the book, there's a special chapter just about these questions. When you scale up, you get a lot of people and a lot of money and everything is happening at the same time. So there you need a order of evaluating ideas in a very systematic way. In a company like Netflix, by the way I don't know if they need this specific method. They're very-
turns.zh: 绝对同意。我认为我们讨论的北极星指标（North Star Metric）概念，即创造的价值与捕获的价值之间的关系，对每家公司都非常重要。构建完整的指标体系树，或许有些过头了，在早期阶段就实施严格的OKR（目标与关键结果）体系也可能适得其反。早期阶段的公司甚至尚不清楚如何创造价值，因此需要不断迭代，其核心目标是找到产品与市场的契合点。之后，当公司规模扩大时，就需要着手构建商业模式。这就是你的目标，你要朝着这个目标不断迭代，并为此制定指标。等公司进入扩张阶段后，你需要尝试建立一套有序的评估体系。毕竟，当公司规模扩大时，你会面临大量人员和资金涌入，各种事务同时涌现的情况。此时，就需要用系统化的方法对创意进行评估。顺便说一句，我不确定Netflix是否需要这种特定方法。他们在产品开发方面做得相当出色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, maybe that was a bad example. They're probably doing things pretty well.
turns.zh: 是啊，或许我举了个不好的例子。他们很可能做得很不错。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: One thing I discovered by the way, there's two types of companies that really benefit from this technique. One is those companies that are kind of emerging into modern product development. They have product teams, they have product managers, they have OKRs, they're starting to do Agile. But they're starting to do experimentation, but they're struggling to put it all together. Every CPO is building their own little framework and the other type is those companies that used to be evidence guided and they regressed and that happens way too often. Change of management, change of culture, and then all of a sudden they need to rediscover, to rekindle that spirit that was lost along Google+. So some of the people that actually respond to the strongest are actually surprisingly in these companies.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，我发现有两类公司能真正从这种技术中受益。一类是那些正在向现代产品开发模式转型的公司。他们有产品团队、产品经理、OKR，开始采用敏捷方法，但在整合这些元素时遇到困难。每位首席产品官都在构建自己的小框架。另一类是那些曾经以证据为导向但后来退步的公司，这种情况太常见了。管理层变更、文化转变，突然间他们需要重新发现、重新点燃在Google+时代失去的精神火花。因此，那些对这种方法反应最强烈的人，往往出乎意料地来自这类公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I love about your frameworks and kind of all these things we're talking about is these are just a... You can almost think of them as a grab bag set of tools to make you more evidence guided as a company. You could start with thinking about the confidence meter, you could start using ICE more. You could start using the metrics tree and all these things just push you closer and closer to being more evidence guided, you don't have to adopt this whole thing all at once.
turns.zh: 我喜欢你们的框架以及我们讨论的所有这些东西，它们就像……你几乎可以把它们看作是一套工具组合，帮助公司变得更加以证据为导向。你可以从思考信心指标开始，更多地使用ICE方法，使用指标树等等。所有这些都将一步步推动你朝着更加以证据为导向的方向发展，你不必一口气把整个体系都采用下来。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: Absolutely. I would recommend that you don't try because if the transformation is way too big, you will get fatigued and you will just create a lot of process for a lot of people and you would not see the results and after a quarter you'll give up. So exactly what you suggested is the right approach.
turns.zh: 绝对同意。我建议大家不要急于求全，因为如果变革幅度过大，大家会感到疲惫不堪，只会为很多人增加大量流程，却看不到效果，过了一个季度就放弃了。所以你提出的方法正是正确的做法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What would be the first thing you'd suggest if people were trying to move closer to being less opinion oriented and more evidence-based? Which of these frameworks or models would you recommend first?
turns.zh: 如果人们想更少依赖个人观点，更多以证据为导向，你会首先建议什么？你会首先推荐哪种框架或模型？

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: I recommend that they discuss internally where is the biggest problem that they're facing. If the goals are unclear, there's misalignment, we keep chasing the wrong things, start at the goals layer. Try to establish your North Star metric, your top business metric, your metrics trees, start assigning teams with their own area of responsibility. If you're spending a lot of time in debates and you're constantly fighting and changing your mind. Start with the ideas there and establish impact is confidence or whatever prioritization model you like, but involve evidence in it. I think the confidence meter is a good tool to use irrespective. If you're building too much and you're not learning enough, start adopting the steps layer which we haven't seen yet and if your team is very disengaged. You have one of these teams where the developers are very into Agile, very into quality, very into launching things, start working on the tasks there.
turns.zh: 我建议他们内部讨论当前面临的最大问题。如果目标不明确、团队执行不一致、我们一直在追逐错误的方向，那就从目标层面入手。尝试确立北极星指标、核心业务指标和指标体系，开始为各团队分配专属责任领域。如果大家花费大量时间争论不休、不断反复决策，那就从创意层面着手，通过影响力评估或任何你青睐的优先级模型来明确方向，但务必以数据为支撑。我认为无论如何，信心评估模型都是一个很好的工具。如果开发进度过快但学习不足，就可以引入我们尚未探讨的步骤层面；如果团队积极性低落，特别是那些痴迷于敏捷开发、质量把控和快速上线的新兴团队，那就着手处理他们的任务管理问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, let's keep going.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，我们继续。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: All right, so steps. Steps are about kind of helping us learn and build at the same time as we said and one of the patterns I see is that organizations don't know that they can actually learn at a much lower cost. They believe they need to build this elaborate MVP which is not minimal in any way and then launch it and then they will discover it and basically it's what we used to call beta 20 years ago but just with a different name. What I'm trying to do here in the steps layer is to help companies realize there's a gamut of ways to validate your ideas or more specifically to validate the assumptions in your idea and I created a little model for this, it's called after assessment fact finding, tests, experiments and release results. But again, it's just putting together things that much smarter people invented. So in assessment you have very easy things, things that don't require a lot of work. You check if it aligns with the goals, this idea that you have in your hand. (00:51:14): You do maybe some business modeling, you do ICE analysis, you do Assumption Mapping which is great tool by, David J. Blend, or you talk to your stakeholders one-on-one just to see if there are any risks, etc. These are usually not expensive things and they can teach you an awful lot about the impact and the ease of your idea. The next step is to dig data and usually that goes hand in hand with this. So you can find data in your data analysis through surveys, through competitive analysis, through user interviews and through field research, observing your users. Obviously these last two are pretty expensive, so it's often good not to wait until you have the idea and then start doing your research. It's best to keep doing your research ongoing and then you have some sort of data to lie on and to compare your idea against. But until now we didn't build anything, now you're ready to start testing, building versions of the product and putting them in front of users and measuring the results. But initially you don't build anything, you fake it. (00:52:18): You do a fake door test, you do a smoke test, Wizard of Oz test, a concierge test, usability test. We used a lot of those in the tabbed inbox by the way, one of the first early versions was actually we showed the tabbed inbox working to people. But it wasn't really Gmail, it was just a facade of HTML and behind the scenes and according to the permissions that the users gave us. Some of us moved just the subject and the sender into the right place. So initially the interviewer distracted them and then showed them their inbox and in it the top 50 messages were sorted to the right place, more or less if we got it right and people were like, "Wow, this is actually very cool." And that gave us a lot of evidence.
turns.zh:
好的，接下来是步骤部分。正如我们之前所说，步骤能帮助我们边学习边构建。我发现的一个常见问题是，许多组织并不清楚其实可以以更低成本学习。他们总觉得必须打造一个复杂的MVP（最小可行产品），然后上线，再通过用户反馈进行调整。这其实就是20年前我们所说的Beta测试，只是换了个名字而已。我在步骤层面要做的，就是帮助企业认识到，验证想法或更准确地说验证假设有多种方式。我为此创建了一个模型，叫做“评估-调研-测试-实验-发布结果”。不过说白了，这些方法都是更聪明的人已经发明出来的，我们只是把它们整合起来。

在评估阶段，有很多简单易行的方法，不需要耗费大量精力。比如检查想法是否与目标一致，进行商业建模、ICE分析、假设映射（David J. Blend开发的优秀工具），或者与利益相关者一对一交流，排查风险等。这些成本不高，却能快速了解想法的影响力和可行性。

接下来是数据挖掘，通常与评估同步进行。数据来源包括调查、竞品分析、用户访谈和实地研究。后两者成本较高，因此不必等到想法成型再去调研。持续收集数据并与原始假设对比至关重要。

现在我们要开始测试了，先制作产品版本并让用户试用。初期可以用“假门测试”、“烟雾测试”、“魔术师测试”和“礼宾测试”来验证。例如，我们在标签式收件箱项目中就用了这些方法。最初的版本只是HTML界面模拟，用户授权后我们将主题和发件人信息正确排序。测试时，研究人员先转移用户注意力，再展示整理后的收件箱，用户反馈非常惊喜。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an awesome story. So that was in the user research, it wasn't rolled out to people? It was a manual individual?
turns.zh: 这真是个很棒的故事。那么用户研究阶段的测试没有面向公众吗？只是手动测试个别用户？

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: There wasn't a single line of code written, this was just cooked up by the researchers and our designers. But it gave us some evidence to go and say, we should try and build this thing.
turns.zh: 没有写一行代码，全是研究团队和设计师临时拼凑的。但这些证据让我们确信应该开发这个产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Love that.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: So initially you fake it, mid-level tests are about building a rough version of it, it's not complete, it's not polished, it's not scalable, but it's good enough to give to users to start using. So those are early adopter programs, alphas, longitudinal user studies and fish food. Fish food is testing on your own team.
turns.zh: 起初，你会先做一些伪装测试。中级测试阶段是构建一个初步版本，虽然它还不完善、不够精良、缺乏可扩展性，但至少能让用户开始使用。这类测试通常包括早期用户计划、α测试、纵向用户研究以及内部测试。内部测试又被称为"鱼食测试"。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fish food? I haven't heard that term before. So it's dog fooding, but more local to your team.
turns.zh: 鱼食测试？我之前没听过这个术语。听起来像是自家团队内部测试？

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: I think it's a Googly thing, but some people told me that they use fish food as well in their company the name. So I'm using it, I don't know if there's a better name for it.
turns.zh: 这可能源自谷歌的内部术语，但有人告诉我，他们公司也用"鱼食测试"这个名字来指代内部测试。所以我沿用了这个说法，但不确定是否有更合适的名称。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I wonder why it's called fish food, because it's like little? It's like little gentle little clicks?
turns.zh: 我想知道为什么叫鱼食测试？因为它听起来像是小规模测试？比如一些小的、温和的改进？

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: It could be. Yeah, I don't know.
turns.zh: 有可能吧。嗯，我也不确定。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Okay, super cool. I'm learning a lot here.
turns.zh: 哇，太棒了。我在这儿学到了好多。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: So the next stage is to actually build a kind of more complete version of this and then you can dog food it, then you can give this to your users internally. When I joined Microsoft many years ago, the first thing I noticed was that Outlook was very buggy and I asked people what's going on? And they told me we are all dog fooding the next version of Outlook that hasn't come out yet and that's a very common practice in Silicon Valley. You can do previews, you can do betas, you can do labs, so those are tests. Now, there's a special class of tests which are experiments because they have a control element. So AB tests, multivariate tests, those are all experiments. I'm using the word experiment the way data scientists use it, although people tend to call experiments to everything that you see here and finally, even the release you can do stage release, you can do percent launches, you can do hold backs. All of these things help you further validate your assumptions. Sometimes you need to roll back and change things, but it's another opportunity to learn. (00:55:06): So the key point is you don't have to start at the right-hand side, which is expensive. You can start early on and that leads to poking a lot of ideas very quickly. You realize they're not as good as you thought, and then you can invest more effort into the good ideas. If they generate positive evidence, you can go further and further until that point where you feel you're ready for delivery.
turns.zh: 接下来是构建一个更完整的版本，然后进行内部测试。多年前我加入微软时，第一件事就是发现Outlook漏洞百出，我问大家怎么回事？他们说我们都在内部测试尚未发布的Outlook新版本，而这在硅谷非常常见。你可以做预览、测试版、实验室测试等，这些都属于测试范畴。还有一类特殊测试叫实验，因为它们包含对照组。比如A/B测试、多变量测试等，我这里用的是数据科学家对实验的定义，不过人们往往把所有测试都称为实验。最后，发布阶段可以分阶段发布、按百分比上线、延迟发布等。所有这些步骤都有助于验证假设，有时你需要回头改进，但这也是学习的机会。（00:55:06）：关键是无需从昂贵的右侧入手。你可以尽早开始，这样能快速验证大量想法。发现效果不佳后，再投入更多精力到好的想法上。若能获得积极证据，就能不断深化，最终达到可以交付的阶段。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So we've talked about goals, we've talked about ideas, we're talking about steps here. Is there anything else along steps? And then next I know comes tasks.
turns.zh: 好的。我们讨论了目标、想法和步骤，还有其他相关内容吗？接下来是任务。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: No, this is it for steps. There's a lot more with this, we will not go into all of it.
turns.zh: 没有了，步骤部分就到这儿。不过还有很多相关内容，我们就不一一展开了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, that sounds good. Let's talk about tasks and what you mean there.
turns.zh: 好的，听起来不错。接下来我们谈谈任务，你具体指的是什么？

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: All right, awesome. So in many organizations there's these two worlds. There's the planning world where basically you have the managers, the stakeholders, some of the PMs really sit and think about what we need to launch and that's where we create the strategies and the roadmaps and the projects. But guess who is not invited to the party? The people who are actually doing the work. They live in Agile world, they're very focused on moving tickets to the done state, on completing burning story points, pushing stuff into production and there's a big gap between these two worlds. They don't understand each other, they don't see eye to eye, there's a lot of mistrust being built sometimes against the plans or the managers feels that the teams are just not being very effective. We've seen all of this and the solution, the stop gap is to put a PM in the middle. The PM is supposed to make all of this work, deliver on the roadmap like a project manager, feed the Agile machine with perfectly prioritized product backlogs and stories and it just doesn't work honestly. (00:56:50): And the PMs I meet are very tired and they have to spend so much time in planifications and roadmap discussions and they're very busy, they don't have time to do research or to test ideas. So I suggest changing this and bringing the developers a little bit out of their Agile cage if you like and no disrespect to Agile, it's a great thing but let's let them do more than just develop. Let's let them discover as well and one of the tools I suggest and again this is a process is what I call the GIST board. So it's basically the top three layers of GIST. The goals are on the right, these are just the key results usually per team I suggest not more than four. So you create a GIST board per team, then the ideas we're working on right now sometimes with our ICE scores and then the next few steps that we might want to pursue in order to validate these ideas and this is a very dynamic thing. (00:57:48): It changes all the time, the team leads need to update it and the team needs to meet around it at least once every other week to think to talk about what's going on. Are we still following the right ideas? How are we doing on the goals? What are the next steps? What's blocking us from completing the most important steps? And this is a discussion that is not happening today, because most of the discussion happens at the roadmap level and then there's a lot of discussion at the task level. But this middle layer of what actually are we trying to achieve and how well are we doing on it doesn't exist. If you do have this, you create a lot more context in the minds of your team and then they need to ask you fewer questions. You need to tell them less what to do. They know what's success and they are able to actually do a lot more on their own.
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。在许多组织中存在着两个不同的世界。第一个是规划世界，基本上由经理、利益相关者和一些项目经理组成，他们坐在一起思考需要推出的项目，并在此基础上制定战略、路线图和项目计划。但你猜谁被排除在外？那些真正做事的人！他们生活在敏捷世界里，专注于将任务移至已完成状态，完成待办故事点，将成果投入生产。这两个世界之间存在着巨大鸿沟。他们互不理解，意见不合，有时甚至因计划问题产生不信任，或者经理认为团队效率低下。我们见证过这些问题，解决方案是让项目经理充当桥梁。项目经理本应统筹全局，像项目经理一样交付路线图，为敏捷机制提供优先级分明的产品待办事项和故事，但说实话，这根本行不通。（00:56:50）：我遇到的项目经理都非常疲惫，他们不得不花大量时间参与规划和路线图讨论，忙得不可开交，根本没有时间进行研究或验证想法。因此，我建议改变这种现状，让开发者走出敏捷的"牢笼"——无意冒犯敏捷，它确实很棒，但我们要让他们不仅仅是开发，还要去探索。我推荐的工具之一是GIST看板（GIST board），即GIST模型的上三层。目标写在右侧，通常每个团队不超过四个关键结果。每个团队都建立自己的GIST看板，展示当前正在探索的想法，有时还附带ICE评分，以及接下来要验证这些想法的步骤。这是一个动态的工具，团队每两周至少需要围绕它开会一次，讨论是否仍在正确的方向上推进目标，进展如何，下一步计划是什么，以及阻碍完成关键步骤的因素是什么？而这种讨论现在根本没有发生，因为大多数讨论都停留在路线图层面和任务层面。但中间层——我们真正要达成什么目标，以及进展如何——却缺失了。如果有这个工具，你就能为团队建立更清晰的上下文，他们向你提问也会更少。你只需告诉他们怎么做，他们就能明白成功的标准，并自主完成更多工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is the way to think about the GIST board as the way you should be road roadmapping or is this more of a strategy framework to think about why you should be prioritizing broadly?
turns.zh: GIST看板的思考方式，是否应该被视为路线图规划的方法？还是说它更像是一个战略框架，用于思考为什么要进行广泛的优先级排序？

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: The way I say this is at the beginning of the quarter, the team defines its goals. The leads of the team define the goals, but they review it with the team, they review it with the managers, of course with the stakeholders. Everyone's in agreement, these are the maximum four key results and the one or two objectives you guys need to work on, teams cannot deliver on more than that. You copy these key results into the GIST board, then you start looking at your idea bank or you start generating ideas and say, how can we achieve these key results?
turns.zh: 我要说明的是，在季度初，团队会确定目标。团队负责人会制定这些目标，但会与团队成员、管理层以及相关利益方一起进行审议，确保所有人达成共识。最终确定最多四个关键成果和一到两个需要重点推进的目标，团队不能承担过多任务。将这些关键成果录入GIST看板后，团队便会开始挖掘创意库或生成新想法，思考如何实现这些关键成果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And to clarify the thing you copy is the key result as the goal?
turns.zh: 那我确认一下，您复制的是作为目标的关键成果吗？

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: Yes, exactly. You can write the objectives alongside that to remind people what are we trying to achieve, but the key results are the thing we show here. Then you pick some ideas, the ones that look most promising and as unintuitive as it sounds or counterintuitive as this sounds I would recommend that you let the team pick these ideas. The manager of the stakeholders can propose the ideas, everyone can propose, but the team should use the ICE process to kind of... And especially the product manager is very important here to choose which ideas to test first. Then the team together needs to develop which steps should we run, how can we validate this? Some of the steps will be done by the PM, some by the data analyst, some by the user researcher. But some will involve the team, there'll be some coding, there'll be some running of experiments and so there's some ownership around the steps. A sub team owns each one of these steps and we will change the board very actively. (01:00:24): So if an idea turns out to be bad we will take it off the board and put another idea in this place or maybe we achieve the goal, we don't need to work on this anymore, we can focus something else. So it's a project management tool in a sense.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。可以将目标写在旁边，提醒大家要达成的目标，但关键成果才是我们展示的重点。然后从中挑选最有前景的创意，尽管这听起来可能违反直觉，但我建议让团队自己选择这些创意。管理层或利益相关方可以提出想法，但团队应运用ICE流程来评估每个创意的可行性。产品经理在此过程中尤为重要，需要决定先测试哪个创意，随后团队将共同规划验证步骤。部分步骤由产品经理负责，部分由数据分析师完成，还有些需要用户研究员参与，总之每个步骤都由对应子团队负责，整个过程会动态调整看板内容。（01:00:24）：若某个创意效果不佳，我们会将其移出看板，替换新的想法；若目标已达成，则转向其他方向。这本质上就是一个项目管理工具。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So I'm looking at it and I think maybe the most important piece of this is that steps aren't just like a project, like launch a better onboarding or add the step to onboarding. It's you want to emphasize the steps that you're going to take to get to more and more confidence essentially, and more and more evidence guided thinking versus just, "Well, let's figure out how to launch this feature idea."
turns.zh: 太棒了。我理解最重要的是，这些步骤不应只是项目层面的，比如优化新用户引导流程或添加引导步骤。关键在于要强调通过逐步验证来不断增强信心、获取更多证据的思维方式，而非简单地“想办法上线这个功能点”。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: Exactly. It's not a engineering milestone or a design milestone, it's a learning milestone. So we build something and along the way we actually grow the scope of what we build. We are building the product in the process and we learn, so the two have to come hand in hand.
turns.zh: 没错。这不是工程或设计里程碑，而是学习里程碑。我们边做边学，边建边验证，最终形成产品。两者必须相辅相成。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And for folks that aren't watching this on YouTube, just to walk through an example, we'll do it real quick. So one of your goals here is average onboarding time, you want your goal to be the average onboarding time less than two days, currently five and a half days. An idea there is an onboarding wizard, and then the steps are a usability test with mockups and then a usability test as a prototype and then an AB test?
turns.zh: 对于非YouTube观众，我快速举个例子。目标之一是缩短新用户引导时长，当前平均时长5.5天，目标是降至2天以内。思路是先设计引导流程，再通过模型测试可用性，接着用原型进行可用性测试，最后进行A/B测试？

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: Yeah, basically, and you can alter this as you go along. Sometimes you can run multiple steps in parallel it's not always sequential. But that's basically the process, yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，基本如此。过程中可以并行多个步骤，不一定按顺序推进。但核心流程就是如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So again, what you're trying to emphasize here as a team is just we're not just going to launch this onboarding wizard and we're not going to figure it out later. It's like let's be upfront about the steps we're going to take to build more and more confidence. This is something we should keep investing more and more in, which is really interesting.
turns.zh: 太棒了。所以再强调一下，作为一个团队，我们不只是推出这个入职向导，然后事后再去解决问题。关键在于，我们要坦诚地告知用户，我们将采取哪些步骤来逐步增强他们的信心。这是我们应该持续投入精力的领域，真的很有意思。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: Yeah, and another interesting thing that happens every time you run a step if it's successful you have evidence and you can go back to the managers and tell them and share and say, "With this idea we thought it was great, but we got this result. What do you think that means?" And sometimes that manager that propose it would say, "I think the test failed, let's rerun it." Or sometimes they will say, "Maybe it's not as strong as I thought. The discussion just becomes that much more nuanced and objective if you like.
turns.zh: 是的，每次执行某个步骤，如果成功了，都会留下证据。我们可以回到经理那里，向他们汇报并分享成果，说：“我们原本认为这个想法很棒，但实际效果却不尽如人意。你们觉得这意味着什么？” 有时，提出这个想法的经理会说：“看来测试失败了，我们重新再来一遍吧。” 有时，他们会说：“或许这个想法没我想象的那么强大。” 如果你愿意，这种讨论会变得更加细致和客观。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe just to close out this framework. How does this relate to a roadmap that they may have in a spreadsheet or in Jira or in Asana or something like that. Does this sit on top of that? Is this replacing a roadmap somewhere else?
turns.zh: 或许最后总结一下这个框架。它与用户可能在电子表格、Jira、Asana等工具中制定的路线图有何关联？它是建立在路线图之上的吗？还是会取代其他地方的路线图？

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: I would say that release roadmaps where you are just saying by Q3 we want to launch this or by October we have to launch that, they're kind of competing with this. If you're doing that and people know that the goal is to launch that thing by October, forget about learning, forget about evidence guided, I recommend using outcome roadmaps saying by October we want to achieve this outcome. By Q4 we want to launch in another three countries, or we want to grow our usage in India by that much, by this time we need to tackle the problem of churn and how we achieve this. Sometimes we know we have a concrete idea that is high confidence that we already tested, we switch into delivery, then we can put it on the roadmap and say, "Yeah, we're going to build this thing and we'll aim for October." But otherwise you want to keep it open and the roadmaps can kind of suffocate this process if you decide upfront with low confidence that this particular idea must be launched.
turns.zh: 我认为那种传统的发布路线图，比如“第三季度要上线这个功能，十月份必须完成那个功能”，与这个框架存在竞争关系。如果你还在按照这种方式做事，而人们又知道十月份必须上线那个功能，那就忽略学习和证据导向的思维了。我建议使用成果导向型路线图，比如“十月份要达成这个成果。第四季度要在另外三个国家上线，或者要在印度提升用户量。到那时，我们需要解决客户流失问题并找到解决方案。” 有时，我们已经验证过某个想法，信心十足，转入交付阶段，然后再把它加入路线图，说：“好的，我们要开发这个功能，目标是十月份上线。” 但除此之外，你要保持灵活性。如果你一开始就低信心地决定某个想法必须上线，那么路线图可能会扼杀这个过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So you're proposing people switch the roadmapping practice to this, which is very ambitious. I love it.
turns.zh: 好的。所以你建议人们转换路线图实践，这确实很雄心勃勃。我很喜欢。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: Well, this is not a roadmap. This is just a tool for the team to manage the project, but I have a proposal for outcome roadmaps inside the book.
turns.zh: 嗯，这不是传统的路线图。这只是团队管理项目的工具，但我在书中提出了成果导向型路线图的建议。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, awesome. Okay. So I was going to ask if people wanted to try this approach, the book is the best way to fully understand the framework and how implement it.
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。好的，我本来想问大家是否愿意尝试这种方法，但书中才是全面理解这个框架并实施它的最佳途径。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: That's one way. I have articles, I have resources on my site, but I try to condense much of what we just discussed in a lot more nuance in the book. So if you are interested in that, I would give it a go.
turns.zh: 这是一种方法。我在我的网站上也有相关文章和资源，但我试图在书中用更丰富的细节浓缩我们刚刚讨论的大部分内容。所以如果你感兴趣的话，不妨一读。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Maybe just on the topic of OKRs real quick. How do OKRs connect to all this? It sounds like broadly you kind of assume people will keep working on here's our metric or key results or objectives and then that plugs into this kind of GIST framework.
turns.zh: 太棒了。或许最后快速谈谈OKR。OKR如何与这一切相结合？看起来你大体上假设人们会继续制定我们的指标、关键结果或目标，然后将其融入到这种GIST框架中。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: So the metrics trees, plus your mission, plus the individual missions of the teams give you most of what you need to populate your OKRs. There's of course a process of alignment, top down, bottom up, side to side, which I talk a little bit about as well. OKRs is a very rich topic, but those things are usually the core. There's usually some other OKRs that's about the health of the company, the health of the product, etc. Those are called supplementary OKRs, I talk about those as well. So yeah, I think OKRs are a helpful tool if you like them.
turns.zh: 因此，度量树、你的使命以及团队的个人使命，共同为你提供了填充OKR所需的大部分内容。当然，还有一个从上到下、从下到上、横向协作的校准过程，我也会稍作讲解。OKR是一个非常丰富的主题，但这些核心要素通常是关键。此外，通常还有一些关于公司健康状况、产品健康状况等的补充OKR，我也会提及这些。所以，我认为OKR是一个很有用的工具，如果你喜欢它的话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And just zooming out again. Basically you don't need to take all of these ideas and lump them all together and change the way you work as a business. You can start with picking some of these ideas and starting to become more and more evidence guided. It sounds like this GIST board isn't where you probably want to start, but maybe it's once you have more and more experience using some of these tools or you tell me. Do you sometimes go straight to this way of thinking about the roadmap and the plan?
turns.zh: 再往外看。基本上，你不需要把所有这些想法都整合在一起，也不需要彻底改变企业的运作方式。你可以从选择其中一些想法开始，逐渐变得更加以证据为导向。听起来这个GIST板可能不是你首先应该关注的，但也许当你使用这些工具积累了更多经验后，或者你告诉我后续情况会不同。你有时会直接进入这种路线图和规划的思维模式吗？

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: So it might not be the full board because you're missing some of the pieces, maybe your goals are not as good or your idea prioritization isn't as good. But if your team is very, very delivery focused and sometimes it's also the opposite. The managers are telling them how to build and you want to break this kind of dynamic, you want to create a step backlog. So instead of a product backlog, let's create a backlog of steps which are just validation steps, betas and previews, etc, and that changes the dynamic pretty strongly.
turns.zh: 所以这可能不是完整的板，因为你缺少了一些部分，也许你的目标不够明确，或者你的想法优先级不够高。但如果你的团队非常注重交付，有时情况也会相反。经理们告诉他们如何构建，而你想打破这种动态，创建一个分步积压列表。因此，不创建产品积压列表，而是创建一个仅由验证步骤、测试版和预览等组成的步骤积压列表，这会极大地改变动态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So by the time this podcast comes out, the book will be out. What is the best place to find the book?
turns.zh: 所以当这期播客发布时，书也将出版。哪里能找到这本书的最佳渠道？

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: Hopefully on Amazon, you can search for it. You can go to my site, itamargilad.com and it'll be presented prominently there and there's also the book landings page where you'll find everything you need to know about the book, evidenceguided.com.
turns.zh: 希望能在亚马逊上找到，你可以搜索它。你也可以访问我的网站itamargilad.com，那里会显著展示这本书，还有书籍登陆页面，在那里你可以找到关于这本书的所有信息，evidenceguided.com。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, with that we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 好的，我们现在进入令人兴奋的闪电问答环节。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: Yes, let's go.
turns.zh: 是的，开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 你向别人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: So I'm going to cheat, I'm going to recommend a series of books so two series. One is the-
turns.zh: 所以我要作弊，我要推荐一系列书籍，也就是两套系列。一套是——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cheating is allowed.
turns.zh: 作弊是允许的。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: All right, cool. One, and those are obvious one. One is the series published by SVPG, Silicon Valley Product Group. So INSPIRED, EMPOWERED, now I think TRANSFORMED has come out, I haven't read it yet but I'm sure it's amazing. So this is Marty Cagan and his colleagues, they write some tremendous books and every product manager should read them. The other series, a bit older, this is the Lean series, The Lean Startup, Lean Enterprise, Lean Analytics, there's gold in all these books, Lean UX, really, really important books and I think they're not as appreciated as they should. Running Lean, that's another example.
turns.zh: 好的，很酷。一套是显而易见的。一套是SVPG（硅谷产品集团）出版的系列。《INSPIRED》、《EMPOWERED》，现在我想《TRANSFORMED》也出版了，我还没读过，但我确定它很棒。所以这是马蒂·卡根和他的同事们，他们写了一些很棒的书，每个产品经理都应该读一读。另一套系列稍微老一些，这是精益系列，《精益创业》、《精益企业》、《精益分析》，这些书里都充满了金玉良言，《精益UX》也是，真的非常非常重要的书，我认为它们没有得到应有的重视。《Running Lean》就是另一个例子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 最近最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: I'm not really a big TV or movie buff, I just put on whatever comes up. I'm discovering that YouTube is actually becoming one of my sources of information entertainment. I'm learning a lot of Spanish recently, so I discovered this channel called Dreaming Spanish which is if you're learning Spanish it's incredible. So that's my recommendation.
turns.zh: 我其实不是很热衷于看电视或电影，通常都是随意点开播放。我发现YouTube现在成了我获取信息和娱乐的重要来源。最近我在学习西班牙语，发现了一个叫“Dreaming Spanish”的频道，如果你也在学习西班牙语，那简直太棒了。所以这就是我的推荐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a unique choice, I love it. Favorite interview question you like to ask candidates.
turns.zh: 这真是个独特的选择，我很喜欢。你最喜欢问求职者哪种面试问题？

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: I like to ask them to design something for a niche audience. So a navigation system for elderly people or some sort of laptop for people with vision impairment, etc. So those are good questions to see their customer empathy, their creativity, their ability to evaluate multiple ideas, their ability to find flaws in their own ideas. So there's a lot of room to dig in there and kind of see how this person is thinking as a product person.
turns.zh: 我喜欢让他们为小众受众设计产品。比如为老年人设计导航系统，或者为视力受损人群设计笔记本电脑等。这些问题能很好地考察他们的客户共情能力、创造力，以及评估多重想法和发现自身不足的能力。这里有很多深挖的空间，能真正了解这个人作为产品经理的思维模式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite product you recently discovered that you love?
turns.zh: 最近你发现的最喜欢的产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: It's a cliche, but it's AI. There's a company called ElevenLabs, that do voices and the best voices, synthetic voices you heard, but they can also replicate your own voice so you can create a voice signature. If you're American you can use their kind of default free version or cheap version to replicate your own voice and that could be pretty useful if you need to narrate an audiobook or do some online course. So I'm finding this service very interesting.
turns.zh: 说个老生常谈的，AI。有一家叫ElevenLabs的公司，他们做语音合成，拥有最出色的合成语音技术。但你也可以复刻自己的声音，这样就能创建专属语音签名。如果你是美国人，可以使用他们的免费版或低价版来复刻自己的声音，这对录制有声书或制作在线课程非常实用。我觉得这项服务很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is all part of my big retirement plan, find all of these components together that can replace me eventually. You got AI generating content, we'll have this voice thing. I love it, it's all happening.
turns.zh: 这都是我宏大退休计划的一部分，要整合所有能最终替代我自己的技术组件。比如AI生成内容，再加上语音技术。我超爱这个进程，一切都在推进。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: There's an AI version of you, right? I can ask you questions now with-
turns.zh: 有AI版的你，对吧？我现在就能用它提问——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, there is lennybot.com.
turns.zh: 哦，lennybot.com。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's all part of the plan. Okay. What is a favorite life motto that you repeat most to yourself that you share with others?
turns.zh: 这都是计划的一部分。好吧。你最常对自己重复、也乐于与他人分享的人生格言是什么？

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: That's a big one. Albert Einstein I think said, "Strive not to be a success, but to be of value." And I think that's a great motto for people and for companies. It's something that kind of guides me and this whole concept of the value exchange, etc, is kind of loosely connected to that.
turns.zh: 这很重要。我觉得爱因斯坦说过：“不要追求成功，而要追求有价值。” 我觉得这对个人和公司都是很棒的座右铭。它引导着我整个价值交换的理念等，都与此有松散的关联。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that, that's such a important point for people putting out content online. So many people are just like, I just want to be successful, get followers, here's all these things I'm tweeting and showing and the thing that actually works is deliver value, create valuable stuff that people really value and want. I find the signal for that is, do you find it interesting and valuable? If you're like, "Oh wow, that's really interesting." Oftentimes other people are going to find it interesting. So I love that, great choice, I'm going to look at that one up. Two more questions. What's the most valuable lesson you learned from your mom or your dad?
turns.zh: 我超爱这个观点，这对在网上发布内容的人来说太重要了。太多人只想成功、吸引粉丝，拼命发推、展示各种东西，但真正有效的做法是提供有价值的内容，创造人们真正珍视和需要的东西。我发现衡量标准就是：你觉得它有趣、有价值吗？如果你会说“哇，真有意思！” 那其他人通常也会觉得有意思。所以我超爱这个观点，是个很棒的选择，我要去看看那个频道。最后两个问题。你从父母那里学到的最有价值的一课是什么？

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: I think both of them in their own way, they had relatively modest jobs, teaching or doing other things, but they always strived again to be the best they can and to deliver the most value they can. So it's very connected somehow, maybe I'm seeing the world through this lens. But they kind of taught me to strive to be the best I can at what I do.
turns.zh: 我觉得他们俩都以各自的方式，曾从事过相对普通的工作——教书或做其他事情，但他们始终努力做到最好，为他人创造最大价值。这两者之间或许存在某种共鸣，也许我就是通过这个视角看待世界的。但他们确实教会了我要在自己所做的事情上力求做到最好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The final question, you're Israeli for folks that can't tell. What is your favorite Israeli food that people should definitely check out or I try to get whenever they can?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题，你是以色列人，可能有些人还不清楚。你最喜欢的以色列美食是什么？大家应该去尝尝，或者有机会一定要品尝一下。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: When I arrive in Israel I usually go for shawarma, which is like döner kebab if you know it, it's just better. So if you're in Israel, if you go visit Haifa, which is the city where I grew up definitely check out the shawarma.
turns.zh: 我到以色列后，通常会去吃沙威玛，如果你了解土耳其烤肉的话，那种更好吃。所以如果你去以色列，如果你去海法——我长大的城市——一定要尝尝沙威玛。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Itamar, I hope people got the gist of your book from our conversation. What's the best way to find it? What's the best way to learn about you and reach out if they want to ask any questions? And then also, how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 太棒了。伊塔马尔，我希望通过我们的对话，大家能对你的书有一个大致的了解。如何找到它呢？如何了解你并联系你呢？如果有人有任何问题，怎样才能联系到你呢？

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: To find it you can go to itamargilad.com or to evidenceguided.com, and you'll find a book and you'll find me. Best value to me, try it out, just take some of these ideas, bring them back to your office, talk with your colleagues, say what do you think we should do about this? Just give it a go and reach back to me, tell me I'm easy to find in my website. Tell me what happened I'm really interested.
turns.zh: 要找到它，你可以访问itamargilad.com或evidenceguided.com，在那里你能找到这本书，也能找到我。对我来说，最有价值的是——试试看，把这些想法带回你的办公室，和同事讨论一下，说说你们觉得我们应该怎么做？试试看，然后再联系我，告诉我你们在我的网站上很容易找到我。告诉我发生了什么，我真的很感兴趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Itamar, thank you again so much for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。伊塔马尔，再次非常感谢你能来参加节目。

turns.speaker: Itamar Gilad
turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。
